The origin of the Kumortuli Durga Thakur (idols) dates back to 1757, following the historic Battle of Plassey. When Raja Nabakrishna Deb of the Shobhabazar Rajbari wanted to host a grand Durga Puja to celebrate the victory over Islamic tyranny of Siraj-ud-Daulah, he brought skilled kumors (clay potters) from the Nadia district (specifically Krishnanagar) to Kolkata to sculpt the Deity.

To sustain this artistry, the incoming British East India Company in order to gain public support, and the local royalty allocated a specific pocket of land near the Hooghly River in North Kolkata to these craftsmen. Derived from the Bengali words Kumar (potter) and Tuli (locality), Kumortuli became the official settlement where generations of artisans transformed clay into divinity.

The Evolution of the Idols:-
The British Colonization Era (Post-1757): Originally, Durga Puja was exclusively celebrated by wealthy zamindars (landlords). The potters lived in Kumortuli year-round, making household clay items like crockery to survive the off-season, and shifting to complex idol-making strictly around autumn. 

The Traditional Ek-Chala Style: Historically, the idols were crafted in the ek-chala style, where Goddess Durga and Her four children (Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesh, and Kartikeya) are framed against a single, continuous semi-circular background backdrop.

The "Pal" Lineage: The community of Kumbhakars (potters) who settled here were traditionally bestowed with the surname 'Pal'. Today, their descendants continue to dominate the craftsmanship, preserving centuries-old sculpting techniques passed down through generations.

Sacred Milestones in Making a Kumortuli Idol:-
The creation of the Durga Thakur is tied to strict spiritual rituals-
The Clay Foundation: The inner base is built using straw and bamboo frameworks. It is then layered with smooth clay mixed with fine jute fibers. Crucially, the clay blend includes Punya Mati (sacred soil collected from many places).
Mahalaya and Chokkhudaan: The most vital ritual takes place on the dawn of Mahalaya. The senior artists perform Chokkhudaan (the bestowing of the eyes), where they paint the eyes of the Goddess, symbolically breathing life and divine consciousness into the clay structure.

Today, what started as a seasonal settlement for rural potters has evolved into the world's largest hub for Devi Durga idols. Kumortuli now exports hundreds of magnificent theme-based and traditional Durga Thakurs annually to pandals across India and global Bengali communities overseas.

Created by Kolkata-based artist Chandra Nath Saha, the installation reimagines everyday writing instruments as a striking representation of the goddess. The artwork stands alongside the venue’s main Durga idol and will not be immersed during the customary Visarjan.

After the festival, the sculpture will be dismantled, and its plastic components will be sent for recycling into new products, highlighting the creative reuse of materials.

But in Calcutta, another story was unfolding...one of grandeur, ambition and an extraordinary cultural encounter.

The celebration was more than a religious observance. It reflected the changing realities of colonial Bengal, where wealth, political influence and social prestige increasingly intersected.

Yet, the story comes with a historical caveat. Although the traditional account links Clive to Nabakrishna Deb's 1757 Durga Puja, conclusive contemporary evidence confirming his attendance has not been established. The episode therefore remains a popular historical tradition rather than an undisputed fact.
